body:
Basic requirements for a patent

Under the Patents Act, 1970, an invention must satisfy the applicable requirements of novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability, and it must not fall within an excluded category of subject matter.

Novelty means that the claimed invention is new when assessed against relevant prior art. An inventive step involves a technical advance or economic significance, or both, that makes the invention not obvious to a person skilled in the field. Industrial applicability means that the invention is capable of being made or used in an industry.

These requirements operate together. An old traditional use fails the novelty requirement; a minor change to an existing practice may also fail the inventive-step requirement. An invention that meets these requirements can still be excluded from patentability by a specific statutory provision.

Section 3: what is not an invention

ProvisionSubjectSignificance
Section 3(c)Mere discovery of a scientific principle or something occurring in natureDiscovering a naturally occurring substance is not, by itself, a patentable invention.
Section 3(j)Plants and animals in whole or in part, other than microorganisms, including seeds, varieties and species; essentially biological processes for production or propagation of plants and animalsA naturally occurring plant or conventional plant variety cannot simply be patented under this provision.
Section 3(p)Traditional knowledge or mere aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known componentsExisting traditional knowledge cannot be repackaged as a patentable invention.

Section 3(p) is the provision most directly associated with traditional knowledge in Indian patent law. It prevents patents on inventions that, in effect, consist of traditional knowledge or merely reproduce known properties of traditionally known components.

The exception for microorganisms in section 3(j) should not be read as automatic permission to patent every microorganism. A claimed invention must still satisfy the other requirements of patent law.

Disclosure of the source of biological material

Where an invention uses biological material, the patent specification must meet the applicable disclosure requirements. Section 10(4)(d)(ii)(D) addresses disclosure of the source and geographical origin of biological material used in an invention.

This provision concerns transparency in the patent application. It is not the same as proving that the invention is new, nor does disclosing the source automatically establish that access and benefit-sharing obligations have been fulfilled.

Opposition and revocation

Patent law provides mechanisms to challenge inappropriate grants:

  • Pre-grant opposition: After publication of a patent application and before grant, any person may submit a representation opposing grant on the statutory grounds under section 25(1).
  • Post-grant opposition: A person interested may oppose a granted patent within the statutory period of 1 year from publication of the grant, under section 25(2).
  • Revocation: Under section 64, the High Court may revoke a patent on a petition by a person interested or the Central Government, or on a counterclaim in a patent-infringement suit.

Among the statutory grounds for opposition is that the claimed invention was anticipated by knowledge, oral or otherwise, available within a local or indigenous community in India or elsewhere. This is especially important because relevant traditional knowledge may not originally have appeared in a conventional scientific journal.

Other statutory grounds address failures concerning disclosure of the source or geographical origin of biological material.

Three independent legal questions

A researcher developing a product from a traditionally used plant should distinguish the following questions:

  1. Patentability: Is the claimed invention genuinely new, inventive, industrially applicable and outside the excluded categories?
  2. Patent disclosure: Has the application supplied the required information, including the source and geographical origin of biological material where applicable?
  3. Lawful access and benefit sharing: Were the relevant biological resources and associated knowledge obtained and used in accordance with biodiversity law?

A positive answer to one question does not automatically resolve the others. A new invention can still involve an unauthorized biological-resource transaction, while lawful access does not make a known traditional practice patentable.

Prelims focus

  • Patents Act, 1970, section 3(p): Traditional knowledge and mere duplication of known traditional properties are excluded.
  • Section 3(c): Mere discoveries of things occurring in nature are excluded.
  • Section 3(j): Plant and animal exclusions, subject to the statutory wording concerning microorganisms.
  • Section 10: Relevant source and geographical-origin disclosures for biological material.
  • Section 25: Pre-grant and post-grant opposition, including grounds relating to oral community knowledge.
  • Trap: Disclosure of origin is not identical to obtaining permission or sharing benefits.

[Government of India, Patents Act, 1970, sections 2(1)(j), 2(1)(ja), 3(c), 3(j), 3(p), 10(4), 25 and 64, Intellectual Property India official statutory text, consulted 14 November 2026; Intellectual Property India, Guidelines for Processing of Patent Applications relating to Traditional Knowledge and Biological Material, 2012, consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A claimed invention using biological material faces separate checks for patentability, patent disclosure and lawful access; passing one does not satisfy the others.
pictures.caption: A patent involving biological material must pass distinct legal checks.

title: Indian Patent Law: Safeguards for Traditional Knowledge and Biological Material

body:
Why access and benefit sharing is necessary

Traditional knowledge can guide research by indicating the possible properties or uses of a biological resource. Commercial research may eventually produce medicines, agricultural products or other marketable goods. When a user benefits from resources or associated knowledge supplied by others, questions arise about authorization, recognition and the sharing of resulting benefits.

Access and benefit sharing (ABS) is the legal and administrative approach used to regulate access to biological resources and associated traditional knowledge and to provide for the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from their utilization.

Benefits may be monetary, such as agreed payments or royalties, or non-monetary, such as research cooperation, capacity building, technology transfer or other agreed measures. The applicable arrangement depends on the law and the particular activity; it is not automatically a fixed percentage of every sale.

India's Biological Diversity Act

The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 provides the principal Indian framework for conserving biodiversity, promoting its sustainable use and regulating the fair and equitable sharing of benefits from biological resources and associated traditional knowledge.

The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 came into force on 1 April 2024. The Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 came into force on 21 December 2024. The amended framework and its subsequent applicable rules and regulations form the basis for understanding access requirements as of 14 November 2026.

Which authority regulates access?

India has a three-level biodiversity governance structure:

  • National Biodiversity Authority (NBA): The national statutory authority, including responsibility for activities requiring national-level approvals and regulation of benefit sharing.
  • State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs): State-level bodies that regulate specified activities involving biological resources and advise state governments.
  • Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs): Local bodies responsible for conservation-related functions and documentation of local biodiversity and associated knowledge.

The three levels perform related but different functions. A BMC does not replace the NBA or SBB where statutory approval or registration from another authority is required.

Access requirements under the amended law

The legal requirements depend on who is accessing the resource and the purpose of access. The following distinctions apply to the regulated categories under the amended framework:

ActivityPerson or entity covered by section 3(2)Indian person or entity covered by section 7
Research in IndiaPrior NBA approval generally requiredApproval generally not required for covered domestic research
Commercial utilization of biological resourcesPrior NBA approval generally requiredPrior intimation and applicable SBB approval process
Obtaining intellectual property rights based on covered resources or knowledgePrior NBA approval before grantNBA registration before grant
Commercialization of such intellectual property rightsNBA approval obligations applyPrior NBA approval required at commercialization

The section 3(2) category covers non-citizens, non-resident Indian citizens, entities not incorporated or registered in India, and entities incorporated or registered in India that are controlled by a foreigner. The section 7 category covers persons and entities outside section 3(2). The precise statutory definitions matter.

There are also specific exemptions and qualifications, including provisions concerning certain local communities, traditional practitioners, cultivated medicinal plants, codified traditional knowledge, traditional agricultural practices and other specified activities. These exemptions are not universal. In particular, the exemption relating to codified traditional knowledge should not be mistaken for a blanket exemption for all access to biological resources associated with such knowledge.

Community interests and benefit claimers

The law recognizes benefit claimers in relation to biological resources and associated knowledge. Benefit-sharing decisions can take account of the people or communities connected with the resource or knowledge and the legally prescribed arrangements.

A community's contribution is not limited to inventing a patentable product. Communities may have preserved crop varieties, maintained knowledge of useful plants or conserved habitats over many generations. Benefit sharing recognizes the relevance of such contributions without requiring every knowledge-holder to become a patent owner.

People's Biodiversity Registers and Gujarat

A People's Biodiversity Register (PBR) records information on local biological resources, their uses and knowledge associated with them. It is prepared and maintained through local biodiversity-management processes with community participation.

In Gujarat, the Gujarat Biodiversity Board performs the state-level role. Local BMCs operate at the relevant rural and urban local-government levels.

A concrete example is the Surat Municipal Corporation Biodiversity Management Committee, constituted by a municipal resolution dated 1 October 2020. Its functions include documenting biodiversity and associated traditional knowledge and maintaining the city's People's Biodiversity Register. Surat's register initiative invites information about local flora, fauna and their uses, including medicinal uses.

A PBR is not the same as TKDL. A PBR concerns local biodiversity and associated knowledge, including conservation and management needs. TKDL is primarily designed to make already published Indian traditional medicinal knowledge usable as prior art during patent examination.

Prelims focus

  • Biological Diversity Act: 2002.
  • Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act: 2023; in force from 1 April 2024.
  • Biological Diversity Rules: 2024; in force from 21 December 2024.
  • NBA, SBB and BMC: National, state and local biodiversity institutions.
  • PBR: People's Biodiversity Register, associated with local biodiversity documentation.
  • Trap: An Indian applicant's NBA registration before an applicable IP grant is different from the NBA approval required for commercialization.

[Government of India, Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended by the Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023, particularly sections 3, 6, 7, 21 and 41; National Biodiversity Authority, FAQs, questions 12–14 and 26–31, consulted 14 November 2026; Government of India, Biological Diversity Rules, 2024, commencement provisions; Surat Municipal Corporation, 'Biodiversity Management Committee' and 'People's Biodiversity Register', consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: India's biodiversity framework operates at national, state and local levels.

title: Community Rights and Access and Benefit Sharing in India and Gujarat

body:
The Convention on Biological Diversity

The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) is an international agreement that opened for signature in 1992 and entered into force on 29 December 1993.

It has 3 objectives:

  1. Conservation of biological diversity.
  2. Sustainable use of the components of biological diversity.
  3. Fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising from the utilization of genetic resources.

These objectives are connected. Biological diversity supports human needs and scientific research, but its conservation and use raise questions about who provides resources and who benefits from their utilization.

The Nagoya Protocol

The Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits Arising from Their Utilization is a supplementary agreement to the CBD.

It was adopted on 29 October 2010 in Nagoya, Japan, and entered into force on 12 October 2014.

The Protocol provides a framework for access and benefit-sharing arrangements. It operates through national legislation and applicable requirements rather than granting every individual or community an automatic patent right.

Prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms

Two important expressions are:

  • Prior informed consent (PIC): The necessary permission obtained before access or utilization where the applicable legal framework requires it. The competent authority or relevant knowledge-holder depends on the law and circumstances.
  • Mutually agreed terms (MAT): Conditions agreed between the relevant parties, including the permitted use of a resource or associated knowledge and the sharing of resulting benefits.

For traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources held by indigenous and local communities, the Protocol contains provisions addressing the involvement, consent or approval of knowledge-holders and benefit sharing, in accordance with domestic legislation.

PIC and MAT answer different questions: PIC concerns authorization before access where required. MAT sets the agreed conditions of use and benefit sharing. Obtaining permission without addressing an applicable benefit-sharing obligation may be insufficient.

The 2024 WIPO Treaty

The WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge was adopted in Geneva on 24 May 2024.

Its central mechanism is a patent disclosure requirement. Where a claimed invention is based on genetic resources or associated traditional knowledge, an applicant must make specified disclosures concerning the origin or source of the genetic resources or the relevant indigenous people or local community providing the associated knowledge, according to the treaty's provisions.

The treaty addresses transparency in patent applications and the risk of erroneous patent grants. It is not a general treaty creating automatic community ownership of all traditional knowledge, and it does not replace applicable biodiversity access and benefit-sharing laws.

Status at the content cutoff of 14 November 2026: The treaty had been adopted but was not yet in force, according to WIPO's treaty-status records. Adoption of a treaty and its entry into legal force are separate events.

How the international instruments differ

InstrumentMain concernImportant date
CBDBiodiversity conservation, sustainable use and benefit sharingEntered into force in 1993
Nagoya ProtocolAccess to genetic resources and equitable benefit-sharing arrangementsEntered into force in 2014
WIPO genetic resources and traditional knowledge treatyDisclosure concerning genetic resources and associated knowledge in patent applicationsAdopted in 2024; not yet in force at the stated cutoff

A hypothetical researcher obtaining genetic material for commercial development may therefore face separate requirements concerning national authorization, benefit-sharing terms and patent disclosures. Compliance with an international patent-disclosure obligation does not, by itself, establish lawful access under domestic biodiversity law.

Prelims focus

  • CBD: Opened for signature in 1992; entered into force in 1993.
  • CBD objectives: Conservation, sustainable use and fair and equitable benefit sharing.
  • Nagoya Protocol: Adopted in 2010; entered into force in 2014.
  • PIC: Prior informed consent.
  • MAT: Mutually agreed terms.
  • WIPO treaty: Adopted on 24 May 2024; not in force as of 14 November 2026.

[Convention on Biological Diversity, Convention text, article 1, and treaty history, consulted 14 November 2026; CBD Secretariat, 'About the Nagoya Protocol' and Nagoya Protocol articles 5–7 and 12, consulted 14 November 2026; WIPO, 'WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge', treaty overview, consulted 14 November 2026; WIPO Lex, treaty status and notifications, latest listed notification dated 8 July 2026, consulted 14 November 2026.]
